section.title: Jerusalem the Unfaithful Bride
section.sectionRationale: In the Bible's longest and most searing allegory, God recounts Jerusalem's whole history as a love story turned betrayal: an abandoned infant rescued and raised, taken as a bride and adorned as a queen, who then prostitutes herself to every passing nation and idol with a promiscuity beyond even Sodom's. The allegory is deliberately shocking, using the raw language of covenant infidelity to expose sin's true nature, yet it ends where grace always ends, with God remembering His covenant and making atonement.
section.thesis: Jerusalem's entire history, found abandoned, cherished, adorned, and then unfaithful beyond any surrounding nation, is told as the story of a bride who betrays a covenant of pure grace, so that the depth of her sin has no other adequate measure than the depth of God's committed love; yet even here, grace does not merely match the sin but exceeds it, as God vows to remember His covenant and establish an everlasting one, a promise fulfilled in Christ's love for His church.
section.frameNote: Six movements: an abandoned infant found, told to live, and raised to become a covenant bride; that bride's trust betrayed as she prostitutes herself with idols made from God's own gifts; her promiscuity spreading shamelessly to surrounding nations without even the dignity of payment; the sentence of exposure and judgment pronounced; the shaming comparison to her sisters Samaria and Sodom, whom she has out-sinned; and the astonishing final turn, an everlasting covenant and atonement that outlasts every betrayal.

units.label: Found, told to live, and wed
units.note: an abandoned infant becomes a covenant bride

verses.text: Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying,
“Son of man, confront Jerusalem with her abominations
and tell her that this is what the Lord GOD says to Jerusalem: Your origin and your birth were in the land of the Canaanites. Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite.
On the day of your birth your cord was not cut, nor were you washed with water for cleansing. You were not rubbed with salt or wrapped in cloths.
No one cared enough for you to do even one of these things out of compassion for you. Instead, you were thrown out into the open field, because you were despised on the day of your birth.
Then I passed by and saw you wallowing in your blood, and as you lay there in your blood I said to you, ‘Live!’ There I said to you, ‘Live!’
I made you thrive like a plant of the field. You grew up and matured and became very beautiful. Your breasts were formed and your hair grew, but you were naked and bare.

Then I passed by and saw you, and you were indeed old enough for love. So I spread My cloak over you and covered your nakedness. I pledged Myself to you, entered into a {{berit|covenant}} with you, and you became Mine, declares the Lord GOD.
Then I bathed you with water, rinsed off your blood, and anointed you with oil.
I clothed you in embroidered cloth and gave you sandals of fine leather. I wrapped you in fine linen and covered you with silk.
I adorned you with jewelry, and I put bracelets on your wrists and a chain around your neck.
I put a ring in your nose, earrings on your ears, and a beautiful crown upon your head.
So you were adorned with gold and silver, and your clothing was made of fine linen, silk, and embroidered cloth. You ate fine flour, honey, and oil. You became very beautiful and rose to be queen.
Your fame spread among the nations on account of your beauty, for it was perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you, declares the Lord GOD.

units.label: Trust betrayed
units.note: prostitution with idols made from God's own gifts

verses.text: But because of your fame, you trusted in your beauty and played the harlot. You lavished your favors on everyone who passed by, and your beauty was theirs for the asking.
You took some of your garments and made colorful high places for yourself, and on them you prostituted yourself. Such things should not have happened; never should they have occurred!
You also took the fine jewelry of gold and silver I had given you, and you made male idols with which to prostitute yourself.
You took your embroidered garments to cover them, and you set My oil and incense before them.
And you set before them as a pleasing aroma the food I had given you, the fine flour, oil, and honey that I had fed you. That is what happened, declares the Lord GOD.
You even took the sons and daughters you bore to Me and sacrificed them as food to idols. Was your prostitution not enough?
You slaughtered My children and delivered them up through the fire to idols.
And in all your abominations and acts of prostitution, you did not remember the days of your youth when you were naked and bare, wallowing in your own blood.

units.label: Promiscuity without shame
units.note: shrines in every street, favors given rather than sold

verses.text: Woe! Woe to you, declares the Lord GOD. And in addition to all your other wickedness,
you built yourself a mound and made yourself a lofty shrine in every public square.
At the head of every street you built your lofty shrines and degraded your beauty. With increasing promiscuity, you spread your legs to all who passed by.
You prostituted yourself with your lustful neighbors, the Egyptians, and increased your promiscuity to provoke Me to anger.
Therefore I stretched out My hand against you and reduced your portion. I gave you over to the desire of those who hate you, the daughters of the Philistines, who were ashamed of your lewd conduct.
Then you prostituted yourself with the Assyrians, because you were not yet satisfied. Even after that, you were still not satisfied.
So you extended your promiscuity to Chaldea, the land of merchants, but even with this you were not satisfied!
How weak-willed is your heart, declares the Lord GOD, while you do all these things, the acts of a shameless prostitute!
But when you built your mounds at the head of every street and made your lofty shrines in every public square, you were not even like a prostitute, because you scorned payment.
You adulterous wife! You receive strangers instead of your own husband!
Men give gifts to all their prostitutes, but you gave gifts to all your lovers. You bribed them to come to you from everywhere for your illicit favors.
So your prostitution is the opposite of that of other women: No one solicited your favors, and you paid a fee instead of receiving one; so you are the very opposite!

units.label: The sentence pronounced
units.note: exposure, judgment, and the end of wrath

verses.text: Therefore, O prostitute, hear the word of the LORD!

This is what the Lord GOD says: Because you poured out your wealth and exposed your nakedness in your promiscuity with your lovers and with all your detestable idols, and because of the blood of your children which you gave to them,

therefore I will surely gather all the lovers with whom you found pleasure, all those you loved and all those you hated. I will gather them against you from all around and expose you before them, and they will see you completely naked.
And I will sentence you to the punishment of women who commit adultery and those who shed blood; so I will bring upon you the wrath of your bloodshed and jealousy.

Then I will deliver you into the hands of your lovers, and they will level your mounds and tear down your lofty shrines. They will strip off your clothes, take your fine jewelry, and leave you naked and bare.
They will bring a mob against you, who will stone you and cut you to pieces with their swords.

Then they will burn down your houses and execute judgment against you in the sight of many women. 
I will put an end to your prostitution, and you will never again pay your lovers.
So I will lay to rest My wrath against you, and My jealousy will turn away from you. Then I will be calm and no longer angry.

Because you did not remember the days of your youth, but enraged Me with all these things, I will surely bring your deeds down upon your own head, declares the Lord GOD. Have you not committed this lewdness on top of all your other abominations?

Behold, all who speak in proverbs will quote this proverb about you: 
‘Like mother, like daughter.’

You are the daughter of your mother, who despised her husband and children. You are the sister of your sisters, who despised their husbands and children. Your mother was a Hittite and your father an Amorite.
Your older sister was Samaria, who lived with her daughters to your north; and your younger sister was Sodom, who lived with her daughters to your south.
And you not only walked in their ways and practiced their abominations, but soon you were more depraved than they were.
As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, your sister Sodom and her daughters never did as you and your daughters have done.
Now this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: She and her daughters were arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy.
Thus they were haughty and committed abominations before Me. Therefore I removed them, as you have seen.
Furthermore, Samaria did not commit half the sins you did. You have multiplied your abominations beyond theirs, and all the abominations you have committed have made your sisters appear righteous.

So now you must bear your disgrace, since you have brought justification for your sisters. For they appear more righteous than you, because your sins were more vile than theirs. So you too must bear your shame and disgrace, since you have made your sisters appear righteous.

units.label: I will remember My covenant
units.note: restoration and an everlasting covenant of atonement

verses.text: But I will restore Sodom and her daughters from captivity, as well as Samaria and her daughters. And I will restore you along with them.
So you will bear your disgrace and be ashamed of all you did to comfort them.
And your sisters, Sodom with her daughters and Samaria with her daughters, will return to their former state. You and your daughters will also return to your former state.
Did you not treat your sister Sodom as an object of scorn in the day of your pride,
before your wickedness was uncovered? Even so, you are now scorned by the daughters of Edom and all those around her, and by the daughters of the Philistines, all those around you who despise you.
You will bear the consequences of your lewdness and your abominations, declares the LORD.
For this is what the Lord GOD says: I will deal with you according to your deeds, since you have despised the oath by breaking the covenant.
But I will remember the {{berit_olam|covenant}} I made with you in the days of your youth, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with you.
Then you will remember your ways and be ashamed when you receive your older and younger sisters. I will give them to you as daughters, but not because of My covenant with you.
So I will establish My covenant with you, and you will know that I am the LORD,
so that when I make {{kipper|atonement}} for all you have done, you will remember and be ashamed and never again open your mouth because of your disgrace, declares the Lord GOD.”

berit.gloss: Covenant, a solemn, binding agreement. God's covenant with Jerusalem in verse 8 is pictured as a marriage vow, freely given to an abandoned infant with nothing to offer in return, making her later infidelity a betrayal of pure, unearned grace rather than a broken business contract.

berit_olam.gloss: Everlasting covenant. Even after cataloguing Jerusalem's covenant-breaking in exhaustive, painful detail, God promises not merely to restore the old covenant but to establish a new, everlasting one that cannot be broken again, language the New Testament applies directly to the covenant secured in Christ's blood.

kipper.gloss: To atone, to cover, to make propitiation. The chapter's final word is not merely restoration but atonement, God Himself providing the covering for sin that Jerusalem's own efforts, and even her shame, could never supply, anticipating the atonement finally accomplished at the cross.

basic.context: This is the Bible's longest and most searing allegory: Jerusalem is pictured as an abandoned infant, rescued and raised by God, taken as His bride and adorned as a queen, who then prostitutes herself with every passing nation and idol, using gifts God Himself gave her. The imagery is deliberately shocking and confronting, meant to expose exactly how serious covenant infidelity is, yet the chapter ends with God vowing to remember His covenant and provide atonement.
basic.hermeneutics: This is an extended allegory, not a literal biography, using the ancient Near Eastern language of marriage and betrayal to describe Israel's national history and covenant unfaithfulness. Read with pastoral honesty rather than either sanitizing its graphic imagery or dwelling on it gratuitously, its plain point is that idolatry is not a minor lapse but a deep betrayal of covenant love, and that grace, astonishingly, outlasts even the worst betrayal.
basic.originalLanguages: God's berit, covenant, with Jerusalem begins as an act of pure grace toward an abandoned infant with nothing to offer. The chapter's climax promises not the old covenant restored but a berit olam, an everlasting covenant, sealed by God's own kipper, atonement, providing the covering for sin that Jerusalem's shame and efforts never could.
basic.typology: Jerusalem's rescue as an abandoned infant, adorned as a bride, then unfaithful, anticipates and is answered by Christ's relationship to His church, whom He 'loved and gave Himself up for her, to sanctify her, having cleansed her by the washing of water with the word, that He might present the church to Himself in splendor, without spot or wrinkle', Ephesians 5:25-27, the same washing, clothing, and betrothal imagery used here.
basic.christ: Where Jerusalem receives grace and betrays it, Christ is the faithful Bridegroom who loves His bride even in her unfaithfulness, cleanses her, and presents her spotless, Ephesians 5:25-27; and where this chapter ends with God remembering His covenant and making atonement despite Jerusalem's covenant-breaking, Christ is that atonement in person, His blood establishing the very everlasting covenant this chapter anticipates, Luke 22:20, Hebrews 13:20.
basic.god: God is a covenant-keeping husband whose grace toward Jerusalem begins entirely unearned and continues despite unthinkable betrayal; His jealousy and wrath are real and severe, yet they are the jealousy of a wounded love, not indifferent cruelty, and His final word is not judgment but remembered covenant and atonement.
basic.crossReferences: Hosea 1-3 tells a strikingly similar story of a faithless wife redeemed by a faithful husband. Ephesians 5:25-27 describes Christ's sanctifying, cleansing love for His bride, the church. Revelation 17-19 contrasts the great prostitute Babylon with the pure bride, the New Jerusalem, adorned for her husband. Jeremiah 31:31-34 promises the new covenant this chapter's 'everlasting covenant' anticipates.
basic.oneStory: This is Israel's whole story told as one long love story turned betrayal, an abandoned infant loved, adorned, and unfaithful beyond any surrounding nation. Yet the story does not end in exposure and shame; it ends where the whole Bible ends, with God remembering His covenant and providing atonement, a promise kept fully when Christ, the faithful Bridegroom, gives Himself for His unfaithful yet beloved bride, the church.

context.literary:
Ezekiel 16 is the longest single unit in the book so far, and it is built as a three-act story with a closing legal verdict. Act one, verses 3 to 14, is a history of grace: a foundling is found, told to live, raised and wed. Act two, verses 15 to 34, is a history of betrayal, and it grows by repetition. Each stage opens with the same movement of 'you took' or 'you built' and runs through idols, child sacrifice, shrines in every square, and one foreign lover after another. Act three, verses 35 to 43, is a courtroom scene in which the lovers become the instruments of sentence. The structure of the rest of the chapter answers it: verses 44 to 52 turn the story sideways to the sisters, and verses 53 to 63 close it with a promise.

There are devices that hold it together. The word 'naked and bare' frames the whole: in verse 7 the girl is naked and bare, in verse 22 she forgot that she was, and in verses 37 to 39 she is stripped back to it. The motif of blood does the same, from the 'wallowing in your blood' of verses 6 and 22 to the 'blood of your children' in verse 36 and the 'bloodshed' of verse 38. The refrain 'declares the Lord GOD' marks the turns. Jewelry, clothing, oil, food and silver, listed in verses 10 to 13, reappear in verses 16 to 19 in the hands of idols. The gifts that God lavished become the material of the betrayal, so that the structure of the chapter is a mirror in which each good thing is reflected in the form it was abused.

The chapter ends where its logic seems least to permit, with restoration and an everlasting covenant. The turn comes at verse 60, 'But I will remember the covenant I made with you in the days of your youth,' a sentence that deliberately recalls verse 8. The last verse, 'when I make atonement for all you have done,' gives the last word to God's act, not to Jerusalem's.
context.historical:
The opening verses turn Jerusalem's genealogy against her pride. 'Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite,' verse 3, does not state an ethnic fact so much as a moral and historical one. Jerusalem was a city of the Canaanite hill country before David took it, and Joshua 15:63 says Judah could not drive out the Jebusites living there. The Amorites and Hittites were among the peoples of the hill country, Numbers 13:29, and Genesis 15:16 had spoken of the 'iniquity of the Amorites.' To call Jerusalem the child of such parents is to remind her that nothing in her origins earned election.

The details of the infant's neglect describe the customs of birth at that time: cutting the cord, washing, rubbing with salt and wrapping in cloths were the normal care of a newborn. Their absence says that the child was left to die. Exposure of unwanted infants was a known practice, and the image would have been understood immediately. The marriage that follows is also drawn from custom. 'I spread My cloak over you' echoes the act of a man who claims a woman by spreading the corner of his garment over her, as Ruth asks of Boaz in Ruth 3:9.

The list of lovers traces Judah's actual diplomacy. Egypt in verse 26, the Philistines in verse 27, Assyria in verse 28 and Chaldea in verse 29 correspond to the shifts of alliance through Judah's history: Ahaz sent for Assyria's help, 2 Kings 16:7-10, and Judah's later kings leaned alternately on Egypt and Babylon. Idolatry went along with political treaty, because making an alliance meant acknowledging the other nation's gods. Child sacrifice is not a rhetorical exaggeration. Ahaz sacrificed his son in the fire, 2 Kings 16:3, and Manasseh did the same, 2 Kings 21:6. The prophet's language is graphic because the facts were.
context.canonical:
The marriage between God and His people is among the most persistent images in Scripture, and Ezekiel 16 is its most extended form. At Sinai Israel took vows, 'All that the LORD has spoken we will do,' Exodus 24:7, and the prophets read that covenant as marriage. Jeremiah remembers 'your love as a bride, how you followed Me in the wilderness,' Jeremiah 2:2, and then mourns that Israel 'has gone up on every high hill and under every green tree to prostitute herself,' Jeremiah 3:6. Isaiah laments, 'See how the faithful city has become a harlot,' Isaiah 1:21. Hosea acts the story out in his own household, with the threat of stripping in Hosea 2:3 and the promise 'I will betroth you to Me forever' in Hosea 2:19. Ezekiel 23 retells it again with two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah.

The restoration also has deep roots. Isaiah 54:5-8 tells the abandoned wife that her Maker is her husband and that with 'everlasting' kindness He will bring her back. Jeremiah 31:3 says 'I have loved you with an everlasting love,' and 31:31-34 promises a new covenant. Ezekiel 36 and 37 pick up the 'everlasting covenant' of 16:60, calling it a covenant of peace in 37:26.

The New Testament presents the bride in Christ. Paul says he promised the Corinthians to one husband, to present them as a pure virgin to Christ, 2 Corinthians 11:2, and describes Christ cleansing His bride in Ephesians 5:26-27. The Book of Revelation ends the story with the marriage of the Lamb, 19:7-8, and the new Jerusalem as 'a bride adorned for her husband,' 21:2. The adulterous city of Ezekiel 16 and the bride of Revelation 21 are the two ends of one biblical arc.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel's first aim is to take away the exiles' sense of innocence. Many of them held that Jerusalem's fall was either undeserved or the fault of earlier generations, and the proverb in 18:2 shows the habit of blaming ancestors. The allegory insists that the guilt is Jerusalem's own, and that it is worse than anyone suspected. The prophet is told in verse 2 to 'confront Jerusalem with her abominations,' and the story is the confrontation.

The second aim is to establish the order of grace before the order of law. The chapter does not start with a command that was broken but with a rescue that was unearned. 'Live!' is said before any good or bad deed. The hearers had thought their security rested on their own standing; the allegory says it rested on a husband's pledge made to a child who had nothing. Every later betrayal is therefore a betrayal of a gift.

The third aim is hope that does not cheapen the guilt. Verses 60 to 63 do not say that Jerusalem was not so bad, or that the past does not matter. They promise that God will remember His covenant and make atonement, and that she will remember and be ashamed. The shame is part of the healing. Ezekiel's hearers are meant to hold both: the thoroughness of the sin and the greater thoroughness of the grace.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes God's judgment on a city through the extended image of a marriage. It does not teach how husbands should treat wives, and nothing in it lets a reader justify humiliating or harming a spouse. The stripping, the stoning and the burning of verses 37 to 41 are an account of what the covenant curses would do to Jerusalem through the nations, and God is the judge, not a pattern for domestic behavior. Reading the chapter as a rule for how marital unfaithfulness should be punished gets it badly wrong.

It also does not teach that women are more prone to unfaithfulness or that their sexuality is the problem. The speaker takes a female image because the covenant is a marriage and the people are the bride, and elsewhere in Scripture the same people are called God's son, Hosea 11:1, or His flock. The image has to be held with the literary decision of the prophet in view: it is a metaphor for a nation's covenant betrayal. Pastoral care is needed with readers who have known real abuse, and the passage should be handled in that spirit and not turned into a weapon.

What the chapter does prescribe is exclusive loyalty to God and thankfulness for His gifts. The things that become idols in verses 15 to 19 are good things, beauty, wealth, food, clothing and children. The application is a question to ask of any gift: am I using it to honor the giver or to serve a substitute? Paul's jealous concern for the church in 2 Corinthians 11:2 is the New Testament form of the same demand.

debates.question: What is promised for Sodom and Samaria in verse 53?

views.label: A real restoration that includes the nations
views.case: The verse says, 'I will restore Sodom and her daughters from captivity, as well as Samaria and her daughters.' Read plainly, God promises a reversal for these cities, and Jerusalem is brought together with them. Many link this to the wider hope that the nations will share in Israel's blessing, as in Genesis 12:3 and Isaiah 19:24-25, and to the way verse 61 says Jerusalem will receive her sisters as daughters.

views.label: A rhetorical or ironic restoration that shames Jerusalem
views.case: Others note that the point of the passage is Jerusalem's humiliation, verses 52 and 54, and read the restoration of Sodom as a comparison: Jerusalem's restoration will be no better than that of the city she thought beneath her. The 'return to former state' is then a leveling and not a salvation oracle for Sodom.

views.label: Restoration as an eschatological sign
views.case: A third approach takes the promise as part of God's final plan to renew all that judgment has ruined, with the ruined cities as examples that nothing is beyond His mercy. It leaves the details open, because the text itself does not explain how this will happen.

debates.bearing: Whatever the exact reading, the verse breaks any assumption that Jerusalem's guilt puts her beyond hope, or that her sisters' guilt does. The chapter wants her to learn that mercy, not merit, restores, and that she has no ground for boasting over anyone.

debates.question: What does 'not because of My covenant with you' mean in verse 61?

views.label: The sisters come as a gift of grace, not by the old covenant's terms
views.case: The phrase indicates that Samaria and Sodom are given to Jerusalem as daughters, but not on the basis of the Sinai covenant, which Jerusalem broke. The new relationship rests on the 'everlasting covenant' of verse 60, so the new arrangement is of a different kind from the old.

views.label: Jerusalem has no claim on them
views.case: Others read it more narrowly: the daughters are not hers by right of her own covenant standing. She receives them by God's gift, which is another note of humbling.

debates.bearing: Both readings point to the new covenant as the ground of restoration, which Jeremiah 31:31-34 and Ezekiel 36 and 37 develop. The shape of the promise is grace again, as at the start of the story.

debates.question: Should the harsh and graphic language shape how the chapter is read?

views.label: It is intentional shock that demands honesty about idolatry
views.case: The language is meant to jolt a complacent audience. It deliberately exceeds what polite speech would say so that the hearers feel what covenant betrayal means, and it should be read as the prophet's strategy of unsettling.

views.label: It is a problem to be handled with care
views.case: Some readers find the portrait of a woman stripped and punished deeply troubling, and warn that taking it as a literal pattern or reading the female figure as inherently shameful causes real harm. They urge reading it as metaphor and drawing out its target, which is the nation's idolatry.

debates.bearing: The two concerns can be held together. The prophet's purpose is to expose a betrayal of grace, and a faithful reading attends both to that purpose and to the pastoral care the language requires.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb that drives the chapter is zanah, to prostitute oneself or to be unfaithful, and its forms recur more than a dozen times. In the prophets it is the standard word for religious betrayal, so when the BSB says 'played the harlot' and 'prostituted yourself,' the Hebrew keeps tying idolatry to the marriage image. It is notable that verse 15 says that she 'trusted' in her beauty. The verb is batach, the ordinary word of trust, which is what Israel was to place in the LORD. Trust has been moved from the giver to the gift.

In verse 6 the repeated 'Live!' is chayi, an imperative that expresses a command and a creative word at once. God speaks over the child 'in your blood,' and the phrase 'in your blood' (the plural damim, which in Hebrew can mean bloodshed as well as blood) sets up the later use of the same word for the shed blood of children in verse 36. The first blood is the blood of birth and the second is the blood of murder.

Verse 8 is built from words of marriage. 'Old enough for love' is literally 'a time of love,' the plural dodim, the word of the Song of Songs. 'I spread My cloak' uses kanaf, the edge or wing of a garment, as in Ruth 3:9, and 'I pledged Myself to you' is a verb of swearing, nishba, followed by 'entered into a covenant,' berit. The sequence is oath, covenant, belonging: 'you became Mine.'

Verse 26 calls Egypt 'lustful neighbors,' and the Hebrew is literally 'great of flesh,' a coarse phrase for the Egyptians. Verse 49 gives the sin of Sodom in three phrases: arrogance, 'overfed,' literally 'fullness of bread,' and 'complacent,' from the idea of quiet ease. They did not strengthen the hand of the poor. That is a striking definition, set beside the picture in Genesis 19 of violence and inhospitality, and it shows the prophets read Sodom as a case of comfortable pride.

The closing verses supply the key words. In verse 53 'restore' translates the idiom of returning a fortune, shuv shevut. Verse 60 promises a berit olam, 'everlasting covenant,' where verse 8 had only 'covenant'; the word 'everlasting' is the new element, and Ezekiel 37:26 uses the same phrase. In verse 63 'make atonement' is kipper, the verb of the sacrificial system, and here God is the one who makes it. Psalm 65:3 has the same sense, 'You atone for our transgressions.' The grammar shows that the covering for sin comes from God and not from Jerusalem.

typology.type: The foundling in her blood, Ezekiel 16:4-6
typology.fulfillment: The abandoned infant to whom God says 'Live!' is a picture of an undeserved rescue, and Paul uses the same logic of the people of God: 'God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8. Ephesians 2:4-5 says God made us alive 'even when we were dead in our trespasses,' and Titus 3:5 says He saved us 'not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy.' The correspondence is the order of grace before works. The type falls short in that the infant in Ezekiel is a nation, while the New Testament applies the rescue to every believer by name and with the washing of rebirth.

typology.type: The bridegroom who covers the bride, Ezekiel 16:8-14
typology.fulfillment: God spreads His cloak, washes, anoints and adorns the bride. Ephesians 5:26-27 says Christ cleanses His bride by the washing with water through the word and presents her 'as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle.' Isaiah 61:10 says He has clothed His people 'with garments of salvation,' and Revelation 19:8 says the bride is given fine linen, bright and pure. In Christ the clothing is His righteousness, so it cannot be spoiled or sold. The type falls short because Jerusalem treated the garments as her own to use, while the church's clothing is a gift that keeps her.

typology.type: The everlasting covenant and atonement, Ezekiel 16:60-63
typology.fulfillment: God promises an everlasting covenant and that He will make atonement. At the Last Supper Jesus says, 'This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you,' Luke 22:20. Hebrews 13:20 speaks of 'the blood of the eternal covenant,' and Hebrews 9:12 says He entered the Most Holy Place by His own blood and secured eternal redemption. The promise of Ezekiel 16:63 that God Himself will make atonement is fulfilled in the person of the Son. The type is complete in the sense that God does the work, and it is surpassed in that atonement is made once for all.

typology.type: Sodom and the greater guilt of privilege, Ezekiel 16:48-52
typology.fulfillment: Jerusalem is told that Sodom was less guilty than she. Jesus applies the same measure to the towns that saw His miracles, saying it will be more bearable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for Capernaum, Matthew 11:23-24. Greater light brings greater accountability. Paul adds that where sin increased, 'grace increased all the more,' Romans 5:20. The type does not show the whole truth, because Jesus' warning is about responsibility while Paul's word tells of the grace that outruns it.

study.christ:
Ezekiel 16 leads to Christ most clearly by way of the marriage, the covenant and the atonement, and the connections are made by the New Testament itself. The marriage comes first. Ezekiel tells of a bridegroom who finds an unwanted child and makes her His own. Ephesians 5:25-27 takes the language of washing, presenting and splendor and applies it to Christ and the church: He 'loved the church and gave Himself up for her,' cleansing her 'by the washing with water through the word' to present her as 'a glorious church.' Where Ezekiel's bridegroom bathes the bride in water in verse 9, Christ's cleansing costs Him His life.

The covenant comes second. The 'everlasting covenant' of verse 60 is a promise whose cost is not explained in Ezekiel, and the Gospels explain it. At the table Jesus says the cup is 'the new covenant in My blood,' Luke 22:20, and Hebrews 13:20 names it 'the eternal covenant.' Jeremiah 31:31-34, which sits close to Ezekiel's promise, says the new covenant will not be like the one Israel broke. Ezekiel 16:59-60 states the problem in one contrast: 'you have despised the oath by breaking the covenant. But I will remember the covenant I made with you.' The first covenant is judged and the second is established by the faithful Husband on behalf of the unfaithful bride.

The atonement comes third. Verse 63 says 'when I make atonement for all you have done.' Because God is the one who makes it, the promise needs a way for God to bear what He judges. Romans 3:25 says God presented Christ 'as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood, in order to demonstrate His righteousness.' The Husband who judged the adultery pays for it. This is the gospel's central surprise: the offended party provides the covering.

There is a fourth link in the pattern of the unloved child. The abandoned infant is lifted out of her blood by a word and a hand she did not earn. In Colossians 2:13, God made us alive with Christ when we were dead in trespasses. The story tells the order in which every believer is saved, by being found, spoken to and covered before being able to respond.

There is also a sobering side. Jesus says that Sodom will fare better than the towns that rejected Him, Matthew 11:23-24, because greater light carries greater responsibility. The same Christ who brings the bride to glory warns that privilege can be despised.

A caution about reading. Not every detail of the allegory is a picture of Christ: the lovers, the shrines and the mounds belong to the story of Jerusalem's sin. The Husband of the allegory is God, and the New Testament identifies the Son as the one in whom the Husband's faithfulness is finally and fully shown.
study.god:
The first and deepest thing the chapter shows is a God whose love begins before there is anything to love. The infant is found 'wallowing in your blood,' verse 6, with no beauty and no claim, and He says 'Live!' This answers every assumption that God's favor is earned. Deuteronomy 7:7 says He did not set His affection on Israel because they were numerous, and Ezekiel 16 shows the same love at its most raw. Everything that follows, the washing, the clothing, the crown, is lavish giving, and the chapter makes the point repeatedly that the splendor was His: 'the splendor I bestowed on you,' verse 14.

It shows a God who is a covenant partner in the full sense, who swears, pledges, and enters into covenant, verse 8. This is not a distant sovereign dealing with a client but a husband bound by oath. It is for that reason that Jerusalem's betrayal is so grave, and it is for that reason too that God will not simply walk away. Because He is bound by His own oath, even His anger is the anger of a husband, and not that of an indifferent judge.

It shows a God who is jealous. The word in verses 38 and 42 is the passion of a love that will not share. The chapter is blunt that the jealousy is real and that its outworking is severe: the lovers gather, the city is stripped and burned. Yet the same jealousy 'will turn away' in verse 42, when the sentence has been carried out and He will be 'calm and no longer angry.' His anger has a goal and an end, and it is not an appetite for cruelty.

It shows a God who is just in comparing. The sisters Sodom and Samaria are not excused, but Jerusalem's guilt is measured against theirs and found greater, verses 47 to 52. God judges according to the light given, as Jesus says in Matthew 11:23-24. He is not partial to His own people.

It shows a God who remembers. When Jerusalem 'did not remember the days of your youth,' verse 22, He did. In verse 60 the promise is 'I will remember the covenant I made with you.' God's memory is not passive; it is the commitment to act, as in Exodus 2:24. Isaiah 49:15 says He will not forget even if a mother could. He is the one who does not let the past, even the worst of it, close the door that He opened.

And it shows a God who provides the way of mercy at His own cost, 'when I make atonement for all you have done,' verse 63. He holds justice and love together by taking on Himself the atonement for the offense. For worship, the chapter calls for humility, since we have nothing He did not give, and for wonder, since the One who was wronged is the One who makes it right.

crossReferences.note: A prophet's marriage story in miniature: the faithless wife is threatened with stripping and then wooed again in the wilderness and betrothed forever, in righteousness, justice, loving devotion and faithfulness. Hosea gives the same movement as Ezekiel 16, from betrayal through judgment to a renewed marriage, in a different setting.

God remembers the devotion of Israel's youth and her love as a bride, following Him in the wilderness. It gives the positive memory that Ezekiel 16:22 says Jerusalem forgot and verse 60 says God remembers.

Your Maker is your husband. He forsook the wife for a brief moment and will bring her back with great compassion. It is the gentler side of the same marriage, and it shows how the exile can be understood as a temporary separation within an everlasting love.

Two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, play the harlot from their youth in Egypt and then become the LORD's. It is Ezekiel's second marriage allegory, with the same themes of foreign alliances and idolatry, and it confirms that chapter 16 is not an isolated image.

The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great and their sin is grievous. It is the background to Ezekiel 16:49-50, where Sodom's sin is described as pride, plenty and ease with no help for the poor, and where Jerusalem is told she has surpassed it.

A new covenant that will not be like the one broken by the fathers, with the law written on hearts and sins forgiven. It matches the 'everlasting covenant' of Ezekiel 16:60 and shows how the old covenant's failure becomes the setting for the new.

God makes a covenant of peace with His people that is everlasting, setting His sanctuary among them forever. It uses the same phrase as 16:60 and shows that the hope given at the end of chapter 16 is carried through the rest of the book.

Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word to present her without stain or wrinkle. It is the marriage of Ezekiel 16:8-14 fulfilled, with the washing, the covering and the splendor now accomplished by the Bridegroom's death.

All Israel will be saved, and the Deliverer will take away their sins. Paul's reading of Israel's future as covenant mercy matches the movement of Ezekiel 16:60-63 from judgment to covenant and the removal of sin.

The marriage of the Lamb has come and His bride has made herself ready, given fine linen, bright and pure. The prostitute city of Ezekiel 16 is answered by the bride who is clothed by grace, and the story of the marriage reaches its goal.

study.oneStory:
Ezekiel 16 tells in one chapter the story that the whole Bible tells in many: a God who finds, rescues and weds, and a people who forsake and betray. It answers the question of why the chosen people were judged, and it does so without cancelling the choice. Back in Genesis 12 God called Abram out of a world of idols to make a people for Himself, and by Exodus 19 He had brought them to Sinai 'on eagles' wings' and made them His own. Ezekiel's chapter reads that history as a marriage and a rescue from the beginning, and it lays on the people the weight of what they were given.

The chapter also explains from within why the fall of Jerusalem had to come. Sin in Eden was a distrust of God's word and a reaching for what He had withheld. In Ezekiel 16 the same distrust appears in the form of trusting beauty, treaties and gods instead of the giver. The rise and fall of the monarchy, with Ahaz's alliance and Manasseh's child sacrifice, are the stages of the betrayal that verses 15 to 34 trace. The exile is the covenant curse that Moses had warned of, falling at last.

But the chapter's last movement opens the story forward. A covenant remembered, a covenant everlasting and an atonement made by God Himself are the three promises on which the rest of the biblical story depends. Ezekiel 36 and 37 develop them with the gift of a new heart and the Spirit. Jeremiah 31 names the new covenant. The Gospels show it signed in blood at the supper and the cross, Luke 22:20, and Hebrews says it is the eternal covenant, 13:20.

The story comes to rest in Christ the Bridegroom, who loves His bride, washes her and presents her to Himself, Ephesians 5:25-27. The church is told to live as a bride who is promised to one husband, 2 Corinthians 11:2, and the warning of Jerusalem's history stands as a lesson for her.

It ends in the new creation, where the story is reversed. The harlot of Revelation 17 is judged, and the new Jerusalem comes down 'prepared as a bride adorned for her husband,' Revelation 21:2. The city that once played the harlot is replaced by a city that is the bride, clothed by grace, and 'the marriage of the Lamb has come,' Revelation 19:7. The infant found in her blood becomes the bride at the wedding supper, with no shame left to remember.

sermon.title: No Fidelity Without Remembering (Ezek. 16; 23)
sermon.why: Carson teaches directly and at length from Ezekiel 16, tracing Jerusalem's spiritual adultery from her rescue as an abandoned infant through her promiscuity with surrounding nations, and lands on the astonishing promise of an everlasting covenant in verses 59-63, the exact arc this study follows from grace, to betrayal, to atonement.

quiz.q: How does God describe Jerusalem's origin and earliest condition in this allegory?

options.text: An abandoned newborn, uncared for and left in the open field, whom God found and told to live.
options.note: Verses 4-6 describe this exact scene, God finding and rescuing a despised, abandoned infant.

options.text: A wealthy princess raised in comfort from birth.
options.note: The allegory begins with total abandonment and helplessness, not inherited wealth or comfort.

options.text: A city already famous for its beauty before God's involvement.
options.note: Jerusalem's later fame and beauty are explicitly credited to what God gave her, not an original condition.

options.text: A city founded by faithful worshipers of the LORD from the start.
options.note: Verse 3 explicitly traces her origin to Canaanite, Amorite, and Hittite roots, not original faithfulness.

quiz.q: What does Jerusalem do with the fine jewelry and garments God gave her?

options.text: She uses them to make idols and shrines for prostituting herself.
options.note: Verses 16-18 describe exactly this misuse of God's own gifts for idolatry.

options.text: She stores them faithfully as a memorial to God's grace.
options.note: The text describes the opposite: misuse of the gifts for idol worship.

options.text: She distributes them generously to the poor.
options.note: The gifts are turned toward idolatry, not charitable distribution, in this passage.

options.text: She sells them to fund the temple's true worship.
options.note: The gifts are explicitly repurposed for false worship, not for supporting true temple worship.

quiz.q: How does this chapter describe Jerusalem's unfaithfulness as uniquely shameless compared to an ordinary prostitute?

options.text: She paid her lovers instead of receiving payment, the opposite of a typical prostitute's arrangement.
options.note: Verse 34 states this exact reversal, that she paid a fee instead of receiving one.

options.text: She refused to have any relations with foreign nations at all.
options.note: The chapter describes extensive involvement with Egypt, Assyria, Philistia, and Chaldea, not refusal.

options.text: She only ever pursued a single foreign nation.
options.note: The text describes promiscuity with multiple nations in succession, not a single exclusive relationship.

options.text: She kept her actions entirely hidden from public view.
options.note: The chapter describes very public shrines built in every street and public square, not secrecy.

quiz.q: How does God's assessment of Jerusalem compare her to Sodom and Samaria?

options.text: Jerusalem's abominations exceeded even Sodom's, making her sisters appear more righteous by comparison.
options.note: Verses 47-52 state this explicitly and repeatedly, that Jerusalem was more depraved than either sister.

options.text: Jerusalem was found entirely innocent compared to both cities.
options.note: The passage's entire argument is that Jerusalem was worse, not innocent by comparison.

options.text: Sodom and Samaria were never actually judged for their sins.
options.note: The text explicitly notes Sodom was already removed, verse 50, for her sins.

options.text: The three cities were judged as exactly, precisely equal in guilt.
options.note: The text insists on a clear ranking, with Jerusalem's guilt exceeding both sisters', not equality.

quiz.q: What is God's ultimate promise at the close of this chapter, in verses 59-63?

options.text: He will remember the covenant made in her youth and establish an everlasting covenant, making atonement for all she has done.
options.note: Verses 60 and 63 state this promise directly, the chapter's climactic turn toward grace.

options.text: He will permanently abandon Jerusalem with no further relationship.
options.note: The chapter's final movement is toward restoration and covenant renewal, not permanent abandonment.

options.text: He will restore Jerusalem only, leaving Sodom and Samaria under judgment forever.
options.note: Verse 53 explicitly includes Sodom and Samaria in the promised restoration, not Jerusalem alone.

options.text: He will require Jerusalem to atone for her own sins before any covenant can be restored.
options.note: The text states God Himself makes the atonement, verse 63, not that Jerusalem earns or provides it herself.

questions: The chapter begins with Jerusalem utterly helpless, an abandoned infant with nothing to offer, whom God rescues purely out of grace. Where in your own life did God meet you at your point of greatest helplessness, before you had anything to offer Him?

Jerusalem used God's own gifts, her beauty, wealth, and adornment, to build idols and pursue other loves. What good gifts in your life might you be quietly redirecting toward something other than God?

This allegory is deliberately shocking to convey how seriously God regards unfaithfulness to Him. Does the severity of the imagery change how seriously you take smaller compromises or divided loyalties in your own devotion to Christ?

Despite a record of betrayal worse than Sodom's, God promises to remember His covenant and make atonement. Where do you need to believe that God's grace can reach a failure you assume is too great or too repeated to be covered?

Christ is the faithful Bridegroom who loves and cleanses His unfaithful bride rather than abandoning her. How does being loved this way, not because of your faithfulness but despite your unfaithfulness, change how you extend grace to others who have failed you?

translationNotes.note: 'I spread My cloak over you' reflects an ancient Near Eastern gesture symbolizing a marriage proposal or the assumption of protective, covenantal responsibility, similar to Ruth's request that Boaz 'spread the corner of your garment over your servant', Ruth 3:9.

'Sister' language for Samaria and Sodom does not indicate literal kinship but a shared moral category, cities compared as siblings in guilt and privilege, a common prophetic device for comparative judgment.

'The days of your youth' recalls the covenant first established at Sinai after the exodus, when Israel, like the infant of this allegory, had nothing to offer God except His own prior choice and grace toward her.
